steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
At a high level, a Transformer learns to relate every input symbol (e.g. a word or token) to every other one in order to build rich, context-dependent representations.  Here’s the conceptual flow:

1. Input embedding + positional information  
   • Each token in a sequence is turned into a fixed-length vector (an “embedding”).  
   • Since there’s no built-in notion of order in the attention mechanism, we add a “positional encoding” (or embedding) so the model knows which token came first, second, etc.

2. Self-Attention: the heart of the Transformer  
   • For each position, compute three vectors by linear projections of its embedding:  
     – Query (Q) – “What am I looking for?”  
     – Key   (K) – “What do I offer?”  
     – Value (V) – “What information do I carry?”  
   • Attention weights are computed by taking the dot-product of a token’s Query with every other token’s Key, scaling and applying softmax.  
   • Each token’s new representation is the weighted sum of all Values, where the weights come from those dot-products.  
   • Intuition: each position “pays attention” to whichever positions have keys most relevant to its query.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   • Rather than doing a single Q/K/V projection, we split into several “heads,” each learning a different projection.  
   • Each head performs its own self-attention, yielding diverse views of dependencies.  
   • The heads’ outputs are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model dimension.

4. Position-wise Feed-Forward Network (FFN)  
   • After attention, each position is processed independently by a small two-layer neural network (same weights at every position).  
   • Typically:  
     hidden = GELU(W1 · attention_output + b1)  
     output = W2 · hidden + b2

5. Residual Connections + Layer Normalization  
   • Around both the multi-head attention sub-layer and the feed-forward sub-layer we add:  
     new_repr = LayerNorm( old_repr + SubLayer(old_repr) )  
   • These “skip connections” help gradients flow and stabilize training.

6. Stacking Layers  
   • A Transformer encoder stacks N identical layers of:  
     [ Multi-Head Self-Attention → Add & Norm → Feed-Forward → Add & Norm ]  
   • In the original Transformer (for sequence-to-sequence tasks) there’s also a decoder stack that uses:  
     – Masked self-attention (preventing positions from attending to future tokens)  
     – Cross-attention (attending over the encoder’s outputs)  
     – Feed-forward + residuals

7. Putting It All Together  
   • In encoder-only models (e.g. BERT) you take just the encoder stack, maybe add a classification head on top.  
   • In encoder-decoder (e.g. original “Attention is All You Need”) you feed source text through the encoder, then generate target text step by step in the decoder, where each new token attends both to earlier target tokens (masked) and to all source tokens.

Why this works:  
– Self-attention flexibly captures relationships at arbitrary distances.  
– Multi-head gives multiple “perspectives” on those relationships.  
– Position-wise feed-forward layers inject non-linearity and help mix features.  
– Residuals, normalization, and pre-training (e.g. masked-language objectives) make very deep stacks trainable.  

In short, a Transformer builds deeply contextual embeddings by repeatedly letting every position look at (i.e. attend to) every other, mixing the results, and refining via feed-forward networks. That architecture scales well and forms the backbone of models like BERT, GPT and many others.
